[[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Prince George's County, Maryland|Prince George's County]] executive [[Angela Alsobrooks]] won her first term in office, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former governor [[Larry Hogan]]. She succeeded Democratic incumbent [[Ben Cardin]], who did not seek a fourth term. Alsobrooks became the [[African Americans in the United States Congress|first African American]] and second woman to represent Maryland in the Senate.{{cite news |last1=Sears |first1=Bryan P. |last2=Ford |first2=William J. |title=Alsobrooks makes history in Senate race, as Hogan cannot repeat his magic |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2024/11/05/alsobrooks-makes-history-in-senate-race-as-hogan-cannot-repeat-his-magic/ |access-date=November 7, 2024 |work=Maryland Matters |date=November 6, 2024}} After Cardin announced his retirement, Alsobrooks and Congressman [[David Trone]] emerged as the frontrunners in the Democratic primary. Although Trone heavily outspent Alsobrooks and led most public opinion polls, Alsobrooks won her party's nomination with 53% of the vote after taking a polling lead during the primary's final weeks. Hogan, who entered the race hours before the filing deadline, quickly emerged as the Republican frontrunner and won his party's nomination with 64% of the vote against former state delegate [[Robin Ficker]]. Despite Maryland's status as a reliably Democratic state, the election was considered more competitive than usual due to Hogan's popularity, reputation as a moderate Republican, and opposition to [[Donald Trump]].{{cite web |title=The 10 Senate seats most likely to flip in 2024 |website=[[CNN]] |date=July 20, 2024 |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/07/20/politics/senate-race-rankings-july-2024/index.html}} Alsobrooks was still considered the favorite to win, due to Maryland's heavy Democratic lean and the concurrent [[2024 United States presidential election in Maryland|presidential election]].{{cite news |last1=McCall |first1=Max |last2=Jain |first2=Lakshya |title=Larry Hogan Faces An Impossible Challenge |url=https://split-ticket.org/2024/02/11/larry-hogan-faces-an-impossible-challenge/ |access-date=February 12, 2024 |work=Split Ticket |date=February 11, 2024|quote=Election results from the last decade show that governors are usually very strong candidates: of the twelve that ran for Senate from 2012 onwards, all but Ted Strickland can credibly claim to have overperformed in their races. But no candidate has come remotely close to posting the numbers necessary to overcome the wall of partisanship Hogan faces in Maryland, which backed Biden by 33 points in 2020. The only senatorial challenger to have accomplished something like this in the Trump era was Doug Jones, who faced a scandal-plagued candidate in Roy Moore in a 2017 special election.}} Republicans have not won a Senate race in Maryland since [[1980 United States Senate election in Maryland|1980]]. Hogan's margin was 17 points better than Trump's margin in Maryland, the largest gap between senatorial and presidential margins in the [[2024 United States Senate elections|2024 cycle]], and this election was the closest Senate race in Maryland since [[2006 United States Senate election in Maryland|2006]].{{cite news |title=Larry Hogan's winning streak comes to an end |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2024/11/05/larry-hogans-winning-streak-comes-to-an-end/ |access-date=November 13, 2024 |work=The Baltimore Sun |date=November 6, 2024}}{{cite news |last1=Rakich |first1=Nathaniel |title=Who were the strongest Senate and House candidates of 2024? |url=https://abcnews.go.com/538/strongest-senate-house-candidates-2024/story?id=117522803 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250111064028/https://abcnews.go.com/538/strongest-senate-house-candidates-2024/story?id=117522803 |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 11, 2025 |access-date=January 10, 2025 |work=ABC News |date=January 10, 2025 |language=en}} Hogan carried [[Anne Arundel County, Maryland|Anne Arundel]] and [[Frederick County, Maryland|Frederick]] counties—both won by [[Kamala Harris]] in the presidential race—and became the first Republican to exceed one million votes in a Maryland U.S. Senate election, the highest total for a Republican in the state's history. Despite this, Hogan could not overcome Alsobrooks's margins in the [[Washington–Baltimore combined statistical area|Washington–Baltimore metropolitan area]], and lost the election by nearly 12 points. Alsobrooks's election, alongside [[Lisa Blunt Rochester]]'s [[2024 United States Senate election in Delaware|victory]] in neighboring [[Delaware]], marks the first time that two African American women have served concurrently in the United States Senate.{{Cite web |last=Norwood |first=Candice |date=2024-11-06 |title=For the first time, the U.S. Senate will have two Black women |url=https://19thnews.org/2024/11/us-senate-history-black-women-angela-alsobrooks-lisa-blunt-rochester/ |access-date=2025-08-04 |website=The 19th |language=en-us}} {{TOC limit|3}} == Background == {{see also|Political party strength in Maryland}} At the federal and state level, Maryland is a deeply [[Red states and blue states|blue state]] and one of the most reliably Democratic states in the nation, with [[Joe Biden]] carrying it by 33 points in the [[2020 United States presidential election in Maryland|2020 presidential election]]. Elections in Maryland are dominated by the [[Baltimore metropolitan area]] and the [[Washington metropolitan area|D.C. suburbs]].{{Cite web |date=2020-12-09 |title=Is Maryland growing even more blue politically? Democrats are showing gains in battleground counties. |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2020/12/09/is-maryland-growing-even-more-blue-politically-democrats-are-showing-gains-in-battleground-counties/ |access-date=2023-11-12 |website=The Baltimore Sun}} At the time of this election, Democrats occupied both [[Maryland's congressional delegations#United States Senate|Senate seats]], seven out of eight [[Maryland's congressional delegations#U.S. House of Representatives|House seats]], supermajorities in both houses of the [[Maryland General Assembly|state legislature]], and all [[Government of Maryland#Executive branch|statewide offices]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] had not won Maryland's Class 1 seat since [[1970 United States Senate election in Maryland|1970]]. Although the entry of former Maryland governor [[Larry Hogan]] was expected to make the race more competitive, the winner of the Democratic primary was favored to win in the general election, given that Republicans had not won a Senate seat in the state of Maryland since [[1980 United States Senate election in Maryland|1980]]. The decline of [[split-ticket voting]] in U.S. Senate races was expected to favor the Democrats for this race.{{Cite web|url=https://centerforpolitics.org/crystalball/the-decline-of-senate-ticket-splitting/|title=The Shocking Decline of Senate Ticket-Splitting|date=May 9, 2024|website=Sabato's Crystal Ball|first1=J.
